passages.heading: Overview
passages.body: Private to Specialist: Disciplined Field Artillery Soldiers embody the Army Values and the Warrior Ethos. They are constantly training to perfect the technical and tactical skills required to deliver timely and accurate fires. Their commitment to the mission—never quitting, accepting defeat, or leaving a fallen comrade is proven through synchronized teamwork and clear communication across the fires enterprise. They stand ready to deploy and support the maneuver force with overwhelming firepower, ensuring maneuver commanders can close with and destroy the enemy. Core Competencies: Demonstrate a high degree of proficiency in warrior tasks and battle drills. Strive for technical and tactical proficiency. Mastering leadership starts with internalizing Be, Know, Do: embodying the character of a professional, mastering the necessary intellectual skills, and executing the actions required for mission success. BE: Attributes of Character and Presence "Be" represents the internal qualities that define a leader’s identity and how they are perceived by others. • Character: This is the moral and ethical core of a leader. It involves living the Army Values (Loyalty, Duty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, Personal Courage) and the Warrior Ethos. A leader of character does what is right even when no one is watching, maintaining empathy and humility to support their team's morale. • Presence: This is the outward appearance and professional image a leader projects. It Includes military bearing, physical fitness, confidence, and resilience. A strong presence ensures a leader is visible, approachable, and sets a positive example that inspires trust in subordinates. KNOW: The Attribute of Intellect "Know" refers to the mental and social capabilities a leader uses to make sound decisions. • Intellect: This encompasses a leader's brainpower and knowledge base. It involves mental agility—the ability to adapt to changing situations—and sound judgment to solve problems effectively. It also includes interpersonal tact, which allows leaders to build consensus and recognize individual strengths within their team. DO: Competencies of Leads, Develops, and Achieves "Do" describes the specific actions and skills leaders must demonstrate to fulfill their responsibilities. • Leads: This competency involves providing purpose, direction, and motivation. Leaders influence others by communicating effectively, building trust, and leading by example to achieve the mission. • Develops: A leader focuses on improving the organization and its people. This is achieved by creating a positive environment, coaching, mentoring, and ensuring that subordinates are prepared for future roles. • Achieves: This is the ultimate goal of leadership: getting results. Leaders achieve by integrating all other attributes and competencies to execute tasks, meet the commander's intent, and provide constructive feedback to enhance team performance. By building Soldier proficiencies and fostering tactical knowledge, these educational experiences ensure units are better prepared and more capable. Civilian Education: Planning your college program early is encouraged. To explore your educational opportunities, visit your installation's Education Center. passages.heading: Corporal/Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The CPL was established in 1775 with the birth of the Army and the NCO Corps. Along with the rank of sergeant, the corporal is the only rank that has never disappeared from the NCO Corps. CPLs are the base of the NCO ranks, serving as leaders of the smallest Army units, principally, team leaders. Like sergeants, corporals are responsible for the individual training, personal appearance, and cleanliness of their Soldiers. As the command sergeant major is known as the epitome of success in the NCO Corps, thethe corporal is the beginning of the NCO Corps. As the NCO Corps is known as the backbone of the Army, the corporal and the sergeant are the backbone of the NCO Corps. The Sergeant exercises direct leadership and supervision over assigned teams, functioning as the first line of the NCO Support Channel. As a first line supervisor, SGTs have the most direct impact on Soldiers. SGTs live and work with Soldiers every day and are responsible for their health, welfare, and safety. The counseling, training, and care SGTs provide will determine the success of the unit’s mission and prevent issues from occurring during home station operations. These leaders ensure their Soldiers meet all standards. They teach them to maintain and account for their team members as well as unit equipment. Core Competencies: Readiness: Know your Soldiers and how their individual readiness affects unit readiness. Focus on commander’s key training objectives and own the individual training of your Soldiers that supports readiness. Conduct performance assessments and open and honest counseling of subordinates. Leadership: Demonstrate the courage and moral strength to do the right thing consistent with the Army Values and the Army Ethics. Develop Soldier knowledge, skills, and behaviors. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Training Management: Understand the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and know Soldiers’ abilities to achieve desired training outcomes. Lead effective, challenging, and realistic training. Follow Troop Leading Procedures and the 8-step training model to support the training management process. passages.heading: Staff Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SSG is a critical link in the NCO support channel. As a first line supervisor, SSGs live and work with Soldiers every day and are responsible for their health, welfare, and safety. These leaders ensure that their Soldiers meet standards in personal appearance and teach them to maintain and account for their individual and unit equipment and property. The SSG enforces standards, develops, and trains Soldiers in MOS competencies to accomplish the mission. The SSGs secondary role is to support the chain of command through the NCO Support Channel. Core Competencies: Readiness: Understand, train, and assess individual, team, and squad tasks that fall within unit METL. Develop squad training plans that support the unit METL and are nested with platoon and company training plans. Understand and communicate the importance of readiness, the systems that track it, and the impacts it has on the mission. Leadership: Actions and conduct consistently reflect the Army Values and Army Ethics; remain a role model for Soldiers. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Know your Soldiers at a personal level to promote effective personal and professional counseling. Training Management: Lead tough, realistic, and challenging training. Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and enhances Soldier’s abilities. Implement and enforce policies and standards on training and emphasize the 8-step training model. Communications: Communicate commander’s intent and operational objectives ensuring a shared understanding by subordinates. Employ active listening to gain a thorough understanding of commander’s intent, unit’s mission, and challenges presented by the operational environment. Effectively using written communication when writing narratives, awards, evaluations, and electronic communications. Operations: Understand the commander’s intent and employ principles of mission command to achieve it in the operational environment. Engaged throughout the planning process, assist in and be a part of the planning, preparation, execution, and assessment of training. Be a trainer to increase proficiency of their subordinates (Soldiers and Army Civilians) to prepare to conduct a unit’s wartime mission. passages.heading: Sergeant First Class — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SFC serves at all echelons. The Platoon Sergeant is the senior NCO at the platoon level and primary advisor to the Platoon Leader. They are responsible for the continued professional development and mentoring of the Platoon Leader. The Platoon Sergeant is primarily responsible for the health, welfare, training, and development of the Soldiers in their charge. They are the first level of NCO that has input into the unit's Mission Essential Task List and train collective tasks at the platoon level. The SFC uses their extensive experience and knowledge base to provide input to their superiors for purposes of planning or executing operations. They may also be called upon to train Soldiers on both collective and individual tasks. Core Competencies: Readiness: Proactively address Soldier issues that will affect unit readiness. Prioritize readiness across the formation by forecasting future shortfalls and gaps created by equipment and personnel changes. Understand and teach the impact of Soldier’s individual readiness on the unit. Leadership: Utilize Mission Command to execute the commander’s and platoon leader’s intent through disciplined initiative empowering subordinate leaders. Coach and counsel the NCOs in the platoon, as well as advising and mentoring the platoon leader. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Training Management: Ensure training is properly planned, resourced, rehearsed, and executed. Set and enforce standards during all training events. Ensure Soldiers know and understand commander’s intent, mission requirements, and the reason for the training event(s). Communications: Provide direction, guidance, and clear priorities that support the commander’s intent. Effectively communicate during planning, preparation, and execution. Publicly praise good performance and privately reprimand substandard performance. Operations: Assess the operational environment, leveraging knowledge and experience to understand how it will affect accomplishment of the unit’s mission. Employ the principles of Mission Command to support the commander’s intent. Advise the platoon leader and commander on prudent and acceptable levels of risk during training and operations. Program Management: Conduct continuous performance assessments to ensure the platoon meets the unit mission requirements. Increase maintenance program efficiency by understanding and being actively involved in platoon level maintenance. Ensure the platoon’s individual and collective training records are accurately recorded in the proper system of record ATIS. passages.heading: Master Sergeant/First Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The MSG serves as a key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion or higher levels. The MSG’s level of experience makes them an invaluable member of the staff for input on policy development, training development, and enforcing standards and discipline within the organization. The 1SG is the senior enlisted advisor to the commander at the company/troop/battery level. 1SGs are responsible for maintaining and enforcing standards, ensuring training objectives are met, developing the Soldiers in the unit, all administrative functions, and ensuring the health, welfare, and morale of the unit and their Families. The 1SG serves as a coordinator for training and resources, as well as the lead integrator with outside organizations and entities. Core Competencies: Readiness: Assist the commander in prioritizing AR 350-1 training; enforce the unit’s training program. Advise the commander on Uniform Code of Military Justice actions and manage the execution of the administration process. Implement and manage the unit physical readiness program. Leadership: Assess, create, and foster an ethical and positive culture and climate within the organization. Communicate and drive the commander’s vision and intent by serving as the conduit between the commander and Soldiers. Coach and foster servant leadership through effective counseling and development. Training Management: Design, implement, and manage an NCO leader development program and coach junior officers. Provide oversight of the training management process. Monitor and evaluate individual and collective training in accordance with the unit’s approved METL. Communication: Utilize both oral and written products to effectively communicate ideas, viewpoints, and military correspondence. Employ active listening and the components of communication to solve problems and achieve results. Exercise and enforce emotional intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skill). Operations: Advise commanders and staff; direct the NCO support channel in all operations. Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership to planning and operations. Analyze operational gaps in both the organization and the plan; leverage the shortfalls by providing the appropriate resources and guidance to achieve positive results. Program Management: Train and educate subordinates on Army and organizational programs. Execute talent management. Assist and enforce the standards associated with unit maintenance programs. passages.heading: Sergeant Major / Command Sergeant Major — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SGM is the key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion and higher levels. The SGM is key in the training and operations planning process, leveraging their experience and vast technical and tactical knowledge to advise the staff and the Operations Officer. The SGM is a subject matter expert in their field, primary advisor on policy development, analytical reviewer of regulatory guidance and often fulfills the duties of the CSM in the incumbent’s absence. The CSM is the senior NCO in the command at battalion and higher levels. The CSM carries out, and enforces, policies and standards on performance, training, appearance and conduct of the organization. The CSM is the principal advisor to the commander, giving advice and making recommendations to the commander and staff on matters pertaining to the organization. The CSM is responsible for enlisted talent management and ensures all aspects of the NCO Common Core Competencies (NCO C3) are present in the operational domain. Core Competencies: Readiness: Determine effectiveness of all policies and practices affecting readiness; manage the process. Manage the personnel and individual training components of the Unit Status Reporting (USR). Manage Human Resources to maintain directed levels of individual readiness. Leadership: Develop agile and adaptive leaders who solve problems using critical and creative thinking to sustain an organizational culture that enables Mission Command. Mentor staff NCOs and officers, continually develop their skills to build a stronger staff and planning cell. Extend influence inside and outside the organization through negotiation and utilizing social intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills). Training Management: Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and Soldier’s abilities. Foster an organizational learning culture where opportunities for growth and improvement are enduring. Eliminate or minimize training distractions; discipline the training management process. Communication: Utilizes engaging communication techniques and messages to ensure open communication, solicit feedback from the staff, and remains approachable to foster a positive command environment that supports organizational growth through open and candid communication. Engage key stakeholders and foster strong relationships with agencies within the community to build teams and expand the unit’s sphere of influence. Build relationships with peer units and higher headquarters to champion the unit up and out. Operations: Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership, to planning, and operations. Engage throughout the planning process – Influence planning efforts to reflect reality and true training goals. Ensure leaders are accountable and responsible for the proficiency of their subordinates (Soldiers and Army Civilians) to prepare to conduct its wartime mission. Program Management: Develops, mentors, and manages talent two levels down, based on organizational requirements and assists in subordinates career progression. Shape leaders through talent management efforts that develop NCOs through educational and training opportunities. Enforce effective use of available time to support unit increases in proficiency; actively champion the balance of work/life balance for Soldiers and leaders. Military and Civilian Education: Military Education: Sergeants Major Course (SMC) is your next step in Professional Military Education (PME). Graduating with honors is an excellent way to distinguish yourself from your peers. Additionally, attending courses that enhance your MOS specific individual and collective tasks is vital for preparing yourself and improving your unit's combat effectiveness. Civilian Education: While not a requirement for promotion, possessing a bachelor’s degree and actively working towards a graduate degree is an excellent way to separate yourself from your peers. For assistance with your educational goals, visit your installation's Education Center. Army National Guard of the United States (ARNGUS) Army National Guard Field Artillery NCOs are essential to the Total Force and must meet the same high standards of proficiency and readiness as their Active Army counterparts. Your career path and training opportunities are designed to parallel the active component, ensuring seamless integration during military operations. Equivalent Standards & Training: ARNGUS NCOs must possess the same qualifications, capabilities, and training as Active Army Field Artillery NCOs. Career progression and duty assignments are structured to mirror those in the active component, ensuring you are prepared for any mission. Primary Mission & Readiness: Your primary peacetime mission is to sustain individual and collective training to maintain a constant state of readiness for deployment and combat operations. Focus on perfecting your combat skills and developing your subordinates into a lethal and effective Field Artillery unit. Professional Development: The ARNGUS Noncommissioned Officer Professional Development System (NCOPDS) fulfils all professional development and functional area requirements. While your unit assignments may be influenced by geography, your professional growth path aligns with the standards of the entire Field Artillery community. For specific career progression details, reference the associated MOS chapter for your active duty counterparts. Dual Role as a Citizen-Soldier: In addition to your federal mission, you serve your state and community. You may be activated by your state’s governor to provide support during natural or man made disasters or to assist in Homeland Security missions.

passages.heading: Sergeant Major / Command Sergeant Major — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SGM is the key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion and higher levels. The SGM is key in the training and operations planning process, leveraging their experience and vast technical and tactical knowledge to advise the staff and the Operations Officer. The SGM is a subject matter expert in their field, primary advisor on policy development, analytical reviewer of regulatory guidance and often fulfills the duties of the CSM in the incumbent’s absence. The CSM is the senior NCO in the command at battalion and higher levels. The CSM carries out, and enforces, policies and standards on performance, training, appearance and conduct of the organization. The CSM is the principal advisor to the commander, giving advice and making recommendations to the commander and staff on matters pertaining to the organization. The CSM is responsible for enlisted talent management and ensures all aspects of the NCO Common Core Competencies (NCO C3) are present in the operational domain. Core Competencies: Readiness: Determine effectiveness of all policies and practices affecting readiness; manage the process. Manage the personnel and individual training components of the Unit Status Reporting (USR). Manage Human Resources to maintain directed levels of individual readiness. Leadership: Develop agile and adaptive leaders who solve problems using critical and creative thinking to sustain an organizational culture that enables Mission Command. Mentor staff NCOs and officers, continually develop their skills to build a stronger staff and planning cell. Extend influence inside and outside the organization through negotiation and utilizing social intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills). Training Management: Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and Soldier’s abilities. Foster an organizational learning culture where opportunities for growth and improvement are enduring. Eliminate or minimize training distractions; discipline the training management process. Communication: Utilizes engaging communication techniques and messages to ensure open communication, solicit feedback from the staff, and remains approachable to foster a positive command environment that supports organizational growth through open and candid communication. Engage key stakeholders and foster strong relationships with agencies within the community to build teams and expand the unit’s sphere of influence. Build relationships with peer units and higher headquarters to champion the unit up and out. Operations: Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership, to planning, and operations. Engage throughout the planning process – Influence planning efforts to reflect reality and true training goals. Army National Guard of the United States (ARNGUS) Army National Guard Field Artillery NCOs are essential to the Total Force and must meet the same high standards of proficiency and readiness as their Active Army counterparts. Your career path and training opportunities are designed to parallel the active component, ensuring seamless integration during military operations. Career progression and duty assignments are structured to mirror those in the active component, ensuring you are prepared for any mission. Primary Mission & Readiness: Your primary peacetime mission is to sustain individual and collective training to maintain a constant state of readiness for deployment and combat operations. Focus on perfecting your combat skills and developing your subordinates into a lethal and effective Field Artillery unit. Professional Development: The ARNGUS Noncommissioned Officer Professional Development System (NCOPDS) fulfils all professional development and functional area requirements. While your unit assignments may be influenced by geography, your professional growth path aligns with the standards of the entire Field Artillery community. For specific career progression details, reference the associated MOS chapter for your active duty counterparts. Dual Role as a Citizen-Soldier: In addition to your federal mission, you serve your state and community. You may be activated by your state’s governor to provide support during natural or man made disasters or to assist in Homeland Security missions.

passages.heading: Overview
passages.body: Private to Specialist: Disciplined Field Artillery Soldiers embody the Army Values and the Warrior Ethos. They are constantly training to perfect the technical and tactical skills required to deliver timely and accurate fires. Their commitment to the mission—never quitting, accepting defeat, or leaving a fallen comrade is proven through synchronized teamwork and clear communication across the fires enterprise. They stand ready to deploy and support the maneuver force with overwhelming firepower, ensuring maneuver commanders can close with and destroy the enemy. Core Competencies: Demonstrate a high degree of proficiency in warrior tasks and battle drills. Strive for technical and tactical proficiency. Mastering leadership starts with internalizing Be, Know, Do: embodying the character of a professional, mastering the necessary intellectual skills, and executing the actions required for mission success. BE: Attributes of Character and Presence "Be" represents the internal qualities that define a leader’s identity and how they are perceived by others. • Character: This is the moral and ethical core of a leader. It involves living the Army Values (Loyalty, Duty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, Personal Courage) and the Warrior Ethos. A leader of character does what is right even when no one is watching, maintaining empathy and humility to support their team's morale. • Presence: This is the outward appearance and professional image a leader projects. It Includes military bearing, physical fitness, confidence, and resilience. A strong presence ensures a leader is visible, approachable, and sets a positive example that inspires trust in subordinates. KNOW: The Attribute of Intellect "Know" refers to the mental and social capabilities a leader uses to make sound decisions. • Intellect: This encompasses a leader's brainpower and knowledge base. It involves mental agility—the ability to adapt to changing situations—and sound judgment to solve problems effectively. It also includes interpersonal tact, which allows leaders to build consensus and recognize individual strengths within their team. DO: Competencies of Leads, Develops, and Achieves "Do" describes the specific actions and skills leaders must demonstrate to fulfill their responsibilities. • Leads: This competency involves providing purpose, direction, and motivation. Leaders influence others by communicating effectively, building trust, and leading by example to achieve the mission. • Develops: A leader focuses on improving the organization and its people. This is achieved by creating a positive environment, coaching, mentoring, and ensuring that subordinates are prepared for future roles. • Achieves: This is the ultimate goal of leadership: getting results. Leaders achieve by integrating all other attributes and competencies to execute tasks, meet the commander's intent, and provide constructive feedback to enhance team performance. passages.body: The CPL was established in 1775 with the birth of the Army and the NCO Corps. Along with the rank of sergeant, the corporal is the only rank that has never disappeared from the NCO Corps. CPLs are the base of the NCO ranks, serving as leaders of the smallest Army units, principally, team leaders. Like sergeants, corporals are responsible for the individual training, personal appearance, and cleanliness of their Soldiers. As the command sergeant major is known as the epitome of success in the NCO Corps, thethe corporal is the beginning of the NCO Corps. As the NCO Corps is known as the backbone of the Army, the corporal and the sergeant are the backbone of the NCO Corps. The Sergeant exercises direct leadership and supervision over assigned teams, functioning as the first line of the NCO Support Channel. As a first line supervisor, SGTs have the most direct impact on Soldiers. SGTs live and work with Soldiers every day and are responsible for their health, welfare, and safety. passages.heading: Sergeant Major / Command Sergeant Major — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SGM is the key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion and higher levels. The SGM is key in the training and operations planning process, leveraging their experience and vast technical and tactical knowledge to advise the staff and the Operations Officer. The SGM is a subject matter expert in their field, primary advisor on policy development, analytical reviewer of regulatory guidance and often fulfills the duties of the CSM in the incumbent’s absence. The CSM is the senior NCO in the command at battalion and higher levels. The CSM carries out, and enforces, policies and standards on performance, training, appearance and conduct of the organization. The CSM is the principal advisor to the commander, giving advice and making recommendations to the commander and staff on matters pertaining to the organization. The CSM is responsible for enlisted talent management and ensures all aspects of the NCO Common Core Competencies (NCO C3) are present in the operational domain. Core Competencies: Readiness: Determine effectiveness of all policies and practices affecting readiness; manage the process. Manage the personnel and individual training components of the Unit Status Reporting (USR). Manage Human Resources to maintain directed levels of individual readiness. Leadership: Develop agile and adaptive leaders who solve problems using critical and creative thinking to sustain an organizational culture that enables Mission Command. Mentor staff NCOs and officers, continually develop their skills to build a stronger staff and planning cell. Extend influence inside and outside the organization through negotiation and utilizing social intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills). Training Management: Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and Soldier’s abilities. Foster an organizational learning culture where opportunities for growth and improvement are enduring. Eliminate or minimize training distractions; discipline the training management process. Communication: Utilizes engaging communication techniques and messages to ensure open communication, solicit feedback from the staff, and remains approachable to foster a positive command environment that supports organizational growth through open and candid communication. Build relationships with peer units and higher headquarters to champion the unit up and out. Engage throughout the planning process – Influence planning efforts to reflect reality and true training goals. passages.heading: Overview
passages.body: Private to Specialist: Disciplined Field Artillery Soldiers embody the Army Values and the Warrior Ethos. They are constantly training to perfect the technical and tactical skills required to deliver timely and accurate fires. Their commitment to the mission—never quitting, accepting defeat, or leaving a fallen comrade is proven through synchronized teamwork and clear communication across the fires enterprise. They stand ready to deploy and support the maneuver force with overwhelming firepower, ensuring maneuver commanders can close with and destroy the enemy. Core Competencies: Demonstrate a high degree of proficiency in warrior tasks and battle drills. Strive for technical and tactical proficiency. Mastering leadership starts with internalizing Be, Know, Do: embodying the character of a professional, mastering the necessary intellectual skills, and executing the actions required for mission success. BE: Attributes of Character and Presence "Be" represents the internal qualities that define a leader’s identity and how they are perceived by others. • Character: This is the moral and ethical core of a leader. It involves living the Army Values (Loyalty, Duty, Respect, Selfless Service, Honor, Integrity, Personal Courage) and the Warrior Ethos. A leader of character does what is right even when no one is watching, maintaining empathy and humility to support their team's morale. • Presence: This is the outward appearance and professional image a leader projects. It Includes military bearing, physical fitness, confidence, and resilience. A strong presence ensures a leader is visible, approachable, and sets a positive example that inspires trust in subordinates. KNOW: The Attribute of Intellect "Know" refers to the mental and social capabilities a leader uses to make sound decisions. • Intellect: This encompasses a leader's brainpower and knowledge base. It involves mental agility—the ability to adapt to changing situations—and sound judgment to solve problems effectively. It also includes interpersonal tact, which allows leaders to build consensus and recognize individual strengths within their team. DO: Competencies of Leads, Develops, and Achieves "Do" describes the specific actions and skills leaders must demonstrate to fulfill their responsibilities. • Leads: This competency involves providing purpose, direction, and motivation. Leaders influence others by communicating effectively, building trust, and leading by example to achieve the mission. • Develops: A leader focuses on improving the organization and its people. This is achieved by creating a positive environment, coaching, mentoring, and ensuring that subordinates are prepared for future roles. • Achieves: This is the ultimate goal of leadership: getting results. Leaders achieve by integrating all other attributes and competencies to execute tasks, meet the commander's intent, and provide constructive feedback to enhance team performance. passages.heading: Corporal/Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The CPL was established in 1775 with the birth of the Army and the NCO Corps. Along with the rank of sergeant, the corporal is the only rank that has never disappeared from the NCO Corps. CPLs are the base of the NCO ranks, serving as leaders of the smallest Army units, principally, team leaders. Like sergeants, corporals are responsible for the individual training, personal appearance, and cleanliness of their Soldiers. As the command sergeant major is known as the epitome of success in the NCO Corps, thethe corporal is the beginning of the NCO Corps. As the NCO Corps is known as the backbone of the Army, the corporal and the sergeant are the backbone of the NCO Corps. The Sergeant exercises direct leadership and supervision over assigned teams, functioning as the first line of the NCO Support Channel. As a first line supervisor, SGTs have the most direct impact on Soldiers. SGTs live and work with Soldiers every day and are responsible for their health, welfare, and safety. The counseling, training, and care SGTs provide will determine the success of the unit’s mission and prevent issues from occurring during home station operations. These leaders ensure their Soldiers meet all standards. They teach them to maintain and account for their team members as well as unit equipment. Understand and teach the impact of Soldier’s individual readiness on the unit. Coach and counsel the NCOs in the platoon, as well as advising and mentoring the platoon leader. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Ensure Soldiers know and understand commander’s intent, mission requirements, and the reason for the training event(s). Communications: Provide direction, guidance, and clear priorities that support the commander’s intent. Effectively communicate during planning, preparation, and execution. Publicly praise good performance and privately reprimand substandard performance. Operations: Assess the operational environment, leveraging knowledge and experience to understand how it will affect accomplishment of the unit’s mission. passages.heading: Corporal/Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)

CPLs are the base of the NCO ranks, serving as leaders of the smallest Army units, principally, team leaders. Like sergeants, corporals are responsible for the individual training, personal appearance, and cleanliness of their Soldiers. As the command sergeant major is known as the epitome of success in the NCO Corps, thethe corporal is the beginning of the NCO Corps. passages.heading: Staff Sergeant — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SSG is a critical link in the NCO support channel. As a first line supervisor, SSGs live and work with Soldiers every day and are responsible for their health, welfare, and safety. These leaders ensure that their Soldiers meet standards in personal appearance and teach them to maintain and account for their individual and unit equipment and property. The SSG enforces standards, develops, and trains Soldiers in MOS competencies to accomplish the mission. The SSGs secondary role is to support the chain of command through the NCO Support Channel. Core Competencies: Readiness: Understand, train, and assess individual, team, and squad tasks that fall within unit METL. Develop squad training plans that support the unit METL and are nested with platoon and company training plans. Understand and communicate the importance of readiness, the systems that track it, and the impacts it has on the mission. Leadership: Actions and conduct consistently reflect the Army Values and Army Ethics; remain a role model for Soldiers. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Know your Soldiers at a personal level to promote effective personal and professional counseling. Training Management: Lead tough, realistic, and challenging training. Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and enhances Soldier’s abilities. Implement and enforce policies and standards on training and emphasize the 8-step training model. Communications: Communicate commander’s intent and operational objectives ensuring a shared understanding by subordinates. Employ active listening to gain a thorough understanding of commander’s intent, unit’s mission, and challenges presented by the operational environment. Effectively using written communication when writing narratives, awards, evaluations, and electronic communications. Operations: Understand the commander’s intent and employ principles of mission command to achieve it in the operational environment. Engaged throughout the planning process, assist in and be a part of the planning, preparation, execution, and assessment of training. They are responsible for the continued professional development and mentoring of the Platoon Leader. The Platoon Sergeant is primarily responsible for the health, welfare, training, and development of the Soldiers in their charge. They are the first level of NCO that has input into the unit's Mission Essential Task List and train collective tasks at the platoon level. The SFC uses their extensive experience and knowledge base to provide input to their superiors for purposes of planning or executing operations. They may also be called upon to train Soldiers on both collective and individual tasks. Core Competencies: Readiness: Proactively address Soldier issues that will affect unit readiness. Prioritize readiness across the formation by forecasting future shortfalls and gaps created by equipment and personnel changes. Understand and teach the impact of Soldier’s individual readiness on the unit. Leadership: Utilize Mission Command to execute the commander’s and platoon leader’s intent through disciplined initiative empowering subordinate leaders. Coach and counsel the NCOs in the platoon, as well as advising and mentoring the platoon leader. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Ensure Soldiers know and understand commander’s intent, mission requirements, and the reason for the training event(s). Communications: Provide direction, guidance, and clear priorities that support the commander’s intent. Effectively communicate during planning, preparation, and execution. Publicly praise good performance and privately reprimand substandard performance. passages.heading: Sergeant Major / Command Sergeant Major — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SGM is the key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion and higher levels. The SGM is key in the training and operations planning process, leveraging their experience and vast technical and tactical knowledge to advise the staff and the Operations Officer. The SGM is a subject matter expert in their field, primary advisor on policy development, analytical reviewer of regulatory guidance and often fulfills the duties of the CSM in the incumbent’s absence. The CSM is the senior NCO in the command at battalion and higher levels. The CSM carries out, and enforces, policies and standards on performance, training, appearance and conduct of the organization. The CSM is the principal advisor to the commander, giving advice and making recommendations to the commander and staff on matters pertaining to the organization. The CSM is responsible for enlisted talent management and ensures all aspects of the NCO Common Core Competencies (NCO C3) are present in the operational domain. Core Competencies: Readiness: Determine effectiveness of all policies and practices affecting readiness; manage the process. Manage the personnel and individual training components of the Unit Status Reporting (USR). Manage Human Resources to maintain directed levels of individual readiness. Leadership: Develop agile and adaptive leaders who solve problems using critical and creative thinking to sustain an organizational culture that enables Mission Command. Mentor staff NCOs and officers, continually develop their skills to build a stronger staff and planning cell. Extend influence inside and outside the organization through negotiation and utilizing social intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills). Training Management: Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and Soldier’s abilities. Foster an organizational learning culture where opportunities for growth and improvement are enduring. Eliminate or minimize training distractions; discipline the training management process. Communication: Utilizes engaging communication techniques and messages to ensure open communication, solicit feedback from the staff, and remains approachable to foster a positive command environment that supports organizational growth through open and candid communication. Engage key stakeholders and foster strong relationships with agencies within the community to build teams and expand the unit’s sphere of influence. Build relationships with peer units and higher headquarters to champion the unit up and out. Operations: Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership, to planning, and operations. Engage throughout the planning process – Influence planning efforts to reflect reality and true training goals. Ensure leaders are accountable and responsible for the proficiency of their subordinates (Soldiers and Army Civilians) to prepare to conduct its wartime mission. Program Management: Develops, mentors, and manages talent two levels down, based on organizational requirements and assists in subordinates career progression. Shape leaders through talent management efforts that develop NCOs through educational and training opportunities. Enforce effective use of available time to support unit increases in proficiency; actively champion the balance of work/life balance for Soldiers and leaders. Military and Civilian Education: Military Education: Sergeants Major Course (SMC) is your next step in Professional Military Education (PME). Graduating with honors is an excellent way to distinguish yourself from your peers. Additionally, attending courses that enhance your MOS specific individual and collective tasks is vital for preparing yourself and improving your unit's combat effectiveness. Civilian Education: While not a requirement for promotion, possessing a bachelor’s degree and actively working towards a graduate degree is an excellent way to separate yourself from your peers. For assistance with your educational goals, visit your installation's Education Center. Army National Guard of the United States (ARNGUS) Army National Guard Field Artillery NCOs are essential to the Total Force and must meet the same high standards of proficiency and readiness as their Active Army counterparts. Your career path and training opportunities are designed to parallel the active component, ensuring seamless integration during military operations. Equivalent Standards & Training: ARNGUS NCOs must possess the same qualifications, capabilities, and training as Active Army Field Artillery NCOs. Career progression and duty assignments are structured to mirror those in the active component, ensuring you are prepared for any mission. Primary Mission & Readiness: Your primary peacetime mission is to sustain individual and collective training to maintain a constant state of readiness for deployment and combat operations. Focus on perfecting your combat skills and developing your subordinates into a lethal and effective Field Artillery unit. Professional Development: The ARNGUS Noncommissioned Officer Professional Development System (NCOPDS) fulfils all professional development and functional area requirements. While your unit assignments may be influenced by geography, your professional growth path aligns with the standards of the entire Field Artillery community. For specific career progression details, reference the associated MOS chapter for your active duty counterparts. Dual Role as a Citizen-Soldier: In addition to your federal mission, you serve your state and community. You may be activated by your state’s governor to provide support during natural or man made disasters or to assist in Homeland Security missions.

They are responsible for the continued professional development and mentoring of the Platoon Leader. The Platoon Sergeant is primarily responsible for the health, welfare, training, and development of the Soldiers in their charge. They are the first level of NCO that has input into the unit's Mission Essential Task List and train collective tasks at the platoon level. The SFC uses their extensive experience and knowledge base to provide input to their superiors for purposes of planning or executing operations. They may also be called upon to train Soldiers on both collective and individual tasks. Core Competencies: Readiness: Proactively address Soldier issues that will affect unit readiness. Prioritize readiness across the formation by forecasting future shortfalls and gaps created by equipment and personnel changes. Understand and teach the impact of Soldier’s individual readiness on the unit. Leadership: Utilize Mission Command to execute the commander’s and platoon leader’s intent through disciplined initiative empowering subordinate leaders. Coach and counsel the NCOs in the platoon, as well as advising and mentoring the platoon leader. Create and foster an ethical and positive culture within the unit. Training Management: Ensure training is properly planned, resourced, rehearsed, and executed. Set and enforce standards during all training events. Ensure Soldiers know and understand commander’s intent, mission requirements, and the reason for the training event(s). Communications: Provide direction, guidance, and clear priorities that support the commander’s intent. Effectively communicate during planning, preparation, and execution. Publicly praise good performance and privately reprimand substandard performance. Operations: Assess the operational environment, leveraging knowledge and experience to understand how it will affect accomplishment of the unit’s mission. Employ the principles of Mission Command to support the commander’s intent. Advise the platoon leader and commander on prudent and acceptable levels of risk during training and operations. Training Management: Design, implement, and manage an NCO leader development program and coach junior officers. Provide oversight of the training management process. Monitor and evaluate individual and collective training in accordance with the unit’s approved METL. Communication: Utilize both oral and written products to effectively communicate ideas, viewpoints, and military correspondence. Employ active listening and the components of communication to solve problems and achieve results. Exercise and enforce emotional intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skill). Operations: Advise commanders and staff; direct the NCO support channel in all operations. Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership to planning and operations. passages.heading: Sergeant Major / Command Sergeant Major — recommended career management (applies to every MOS in this career management field)
passages.body: The SGM is the key enlisted member of staff elements at battalion and higher levels. The SGM is key in the training and operations planning process, leveraging their experience and vast technical and tactical knowledge to advise the staff and the Operations Officer. The SGM is a subject matter expert in their field, primary advisor on policy development, analytical reviewer of regulatory guidance and often fulfills the duties of the CSM in the incumbent’s absence. The CSM is the senior NCO in the command at battalion and higher levels. The CSM carries out, and enforces, policies and standards on performance, training, appearance and conduct of the organization. The CSM is the principal advisor to the commander, giving advice and making recommendations to the commander and staff on matters pertaining to the organization. The CSM is responsible for enlisted talent management and ensures all aspects of the NCO Common Core Competencies (NCO C3) are present in the operational domain. Core Competencies: Readiness: Determine effectiveness of all policies and practices affecting readiness; manage the process. Manage the personnel and individual training components of the Unit Status Reporting (USR). Manage Human Resources to maintain directed levels of individual readiness. Leadership: Develop agile and adaptive leaders who solve problems using critical and creative thinking to sustain an organizational culture that enables Mission Command. Mentor staff NCOs and officers, continually develop their skills to build a stronger staff and planning cell. Extend influence inside and outside the organization through negotiation and utilizing social intelligence (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and social skills). Training Management: Ensure training meets the commander’s intent, mission requirements, and Soldier’s abilities. Foster an organizational learning culture where opportunities for growth and improvement are enduring. Eliminate or minimize training distractions; discipline the training management process. Communication: Utilizes engaging communication techniques and messages to ensure open communication, solicit feedback from the staff, and remains approachable to foster a positive command environment that supports organizational growth through open and candid communication. Engage key stakeholders and foster strong relationships with agencies within the community to build teams and expand the unit’s sphere of influence. Build relationships with peer units and higher headquarters to champion the unit up and out. Operations: Extend the operational reach of the commander in all aspects, from leadership, to planning, and operations. Engage throughout the planning process – Influence planning efforts to reflect reality and true training goals. Ensure leaders are accountable and responsible for the proficiency of their subordinates (Soldiers and Army Civilians) to prepare to conduct its wartime mission. Program Management: Develops, mentors, and manages talent two levels down, based on organizational requirements and assists in subordinates career progression. Shape leaders through talent management efforts that develop NCOs through educational and training opportunities. Enforce effective use of available time to support unit increases in proficiency; actively champion the balance of work/life balance for Soldiers and leaders. Military and Civilian Education: Military Education: Sergeants Major Course (SMC) is your next step in Professional Military Education (PME). Graduating with honors is an excellent way to distinguish yourself from your peers. Additionally, attending courses that enhance your MOS specific individual and collective tasks is vital for preparing yourself and improving your unit's combat effectiveness. Civilian Education: While not a requirement for promotion, possessing a bachelor’s degree and actively working towards a graduate degree is an excellent way to separate yourself from your peers. For assistance with your educational goals, visit your installation's Education Center. Army National Guard of the United States (ARNGUS) Army National Guard Field Artillery NCOs are essential to the Total Force and must meet the same high standards of proficiency and readiness as their Active Army counterparts. Your career path and training opportunities are designed to parallel the active component, ensuring seamless integration during military operations. Equivalent Standards & Training: ARNGUS NCOs must possess the same qualifications, capabilities, and training as Active Army Field Artillery NCOs. Career progression and duty assignments are structured to mirror those in the active component, ensuring you are prepared for any mission. Primary Mission & Readiness: Your primary peacetime mission is to sustain individual and collective training to maintain a constant state of readiness for deployment and combat operations. Focus on perfecting your combat skills and developing your subordinates into a lethal and effective Field Artillery unit. Professional Development: The ARNGUS Noncommissioned Officer Professional Development System (NCOPDS) fulfils all professional development and functional area requirements. While your unit assignments may be influenced by geography, your professional growth path aligns with the standards of the entire Field Artillery community. For specific career progression details, reference the associated MOS chapter for your active duty counterparts. Dual Role as a Citizen-Soldier: In addition to your federal mission, you serve your state and community. You may be activated by your state’s governor to provide support during natural or man made disasters or to assist in Homeland Security missions.

passages.heading: Goals for development
passages.body: The primary development goal for Cannon Crewmember is to become technically and tactically proficient leaders capable of executing Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) in a multi-domain environment. Following mastery of core competencies, NCOs should pursue broadening assignments that provide a purposeful expansion of knowledge and skills fundamental to their continued growth and adaptability throughout the career life cycle. passages.heading: Goals for development
passages.body: The primary development goal for Fire Control Specialists is to become technically and tactically proficient leaders capable of executing Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) in a multi-domain environment. passages.body: Major duties: Master Sergeants/First Sergeants are expert leaders and managers of subordinate elements. They master and apply core competencies, unit training, and operational planning. Master Sergeants/First Sergeants possess refined leadership and advisory skills. passages.heading: MSG/1SG — Operational Authorizations
passages.chapter: Chapter 10. 13Z Field Artillery Senior Sergeant/13Z Command Sergeant Major:
passages.body: The career developmental assignment for MSGs is First Sergeant. This position qualifies MSGs to perform duties as the Senior NCO of a unit and enhances their organizational supervisory knowledge, leadership skills, and abilities. MSGs should serve successfully as a First Sergeant for at least 36 months. There is no position in the grade of MSG that provides equivalent leadership training and development. When not assigned as a unit 1SG, the MSG should seek opportunities to serve in Critical Leader Time (CLT) authorizations such as Operations Sergeant within Cannon or Rocket formations across Field Artillery Brigades and Division Artilleries (DIVARTY). Successful performance in these positions is a conditional prerequisite for consideration to SGM.

passages.heading: SGM/CSM — overview
passages.chapter: Chapter 10. 13Z Field Artillery Senior Sergeant/13Z Command Sergeant Major:
passages.body: Major duties: Sergeants Major/Command Sergeants Major must be interpersonal leaders, talent managers, and team builders. They understand and employ concepts and doctrine across multiple domains (joint operations, combined arms maneuver, and joint fires). SGM/CSMs possess exceptional oral and written communication skills. They can conceptualize and devise solutions to complex problems. Prerequisites: All prerequisites are governed by the standards detailed in DA PAM 611-21. Leaders and Soldiers must refer to this publication, accessible via the Army G-1 Publications website, to ensure all requirements are met.

passages.heading: SGM/CSM — Institutional Training
passages.chapter: Chapter 10. 13Z Field Artillery Senior Sergeant/13Z Command Sergeant Major:
passages.body: Institutional Training SGM/CSM development focuses on executive leadership within the Army Leader Development Model. Sergeant Major Academy (SGM-A): Completion of the Sergeants Major Course (SMC) is the baseline for all SGMs. Command Sergeants Major Development Program (CSMDP): Mandatory for all SGMs selected for CSM to ensure readiness for battalion-level command responsibility.

passages.heading: SGM/CSM — Operational Assignments

passages.heading: SGM/CSM — Career Developmental (CSM)
passages.chapter: Chapter 10. 13Z Field Artillery Senior Sergeant/13Z Command Sergeant Major:
passages.body: Successful performance as a Battalion Command Sergeant Major in either the Operating or Generating Force. Force Impact: All SGMs must seek professionally challenging assignments at the Battalion, Brigade, DIVARTY, and MDTF levels. They are expected to provide expert counsel to commanders and make significant contributions to the Branch’s modernization and lethality.

passages.heading: SGM/CSM — Self-Development
passages.chapter: Chapter 10. 13Z Field Artillery Senior Sergeant/13Z Command Sergeant Major:
passages.body: Self-Development SGMs must transition from technical experts to Strategic Fire Support Leaders. Education: SGMs are strongly encouraged to complete a master’s degree or higher. Multidomain Expertise: Leaders must master the entire Fires Kill Chain (Sensor, Control, and Delivery). This requires rigorous self-study of Joint Fires doctrine and the integration of emerging technologies (e.g., PRC-160 HF, Long-Range Precision Fires). Strategic Mentorship: Focus on the mastery of executive-level mentoring and the holistic development of the NCO Corps. SGMs must be the "Masters of Warfighting," capable of operating in Joint, Interagency, Intergovernmental, and Multinational (JIIM) environments.
